question: Did Ibn Taymiyyah deny that Hellfire is eternal?
answer:
As for the issue of Ibn Taymiyyah denying the eternality of Jahannam, this is a very, very interesting and a very detailed and a very controversial topic. And I would love to give a much longer lecture, which is a very advanced lecture, if it were to be given. And in fact, in my master's dissertation, 20 years ago or something, there's an entire section about this issue, because it dealt with whatever topics I was doing.

In a nutshell: did Ibn Taymiyyah hold this view? It is quite clear that he defended the existence of two views in Sunni Islam: one that says Jahannam is eternal, and one that says Jahannam is not eternal. In fact, the last book that he ever wrote, and I have it in my library, the last book that he ever wrote before he passed away, is the refutation of the eternality of Jahannam. Or, and there are different versions of the title, the title is "The issue about the eternality of Jahannam: is Jahannam eternal or not?"

Ibn al-Qayyim mentions this. Ibn al-Qayyim is his main student. "I asked Ibn Taymiyyah about this question: is it true that some of the Salaf denied that Jahannam is going to be forever?" Ibn Taymiyyah said, "Yes, it is true." And then he wrote his famous treatise. And it is a treatise that has been discovered and it has been published recently. And he defends the two opinions, but he doesn't actually say what his own opinion is. So this has left people skeptical.

Now, his student Ibn al-Qayyim has written about this in many, many places. And in fact, in one of his books he has like 10–15 pages about this topic. And in fact, I've written a paper that is published as well about Ibn al-Qayyim's view on this issue, and you can reference it over there. But Ibn al-Qayyim, perhaps in all of Sunni history, is the one who defends this issue of Jahannam not being permanent the most, like, the most detailed evidences he brings to claim that Jahannam is not eternal: that at some stage Jahannam will cease to exist, and the people in Jahannam will cease. And he interprets abada here as meaning a long, long, long, long, long, long time, but not eternal.

And his evidence is Qur'anic and from the Salaf. As for the Qur'an, Allah says ahqaba, and ahqab means long periods of time. So Allah says they will be in it for long periods of time. And Allah also says in the Qur'an that they will remain in it, they will be punished in Jahannam, for as long as the heavens and earth remain. Now, this is an expression in Arabic that means forever. So it means they will remain in Jahannam forever. Then Allah says, "except if your Lord decrees something else. Allah is able to do whatever He wants."

Now, why did Allah end the verses of Jahannam's punishment with this very interesting ending: they shall be in there forever, except if Allah wills, and Allah can will whatever He wants? You see this? Ibn al-Qayyim bases it on this issue. And he does bring this issue as well of Allah's rahmah, etc., etc.

Then, after 10 pages of defending and evidence, and he quotes Ibn Mas'ud (Ibn Mas'ud said this, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said this, Abu Hurayrah said this; there are narrations found in the classical books that eventually Jahannam will cease to exist, from the sahabah, not any hadith from the Prophet), then Ibn al-Qayyim says: "If you were to ask me what my opinion is, I will say Allah knows best." And he left it out there. He did not categorically state. He quoted the Qur'an: "Inna rabbaka fa''alun lima yurid."

So both Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim, and this is my opinion, **seem to be inclined towards the claim that Jahannam is not eternal. But to say that they believed this is also not 100% accurate.** They defended it, yes, and they said this is very plausible, especially Ibn al-Qayyim. They said this is very plausible.

Now, I want to just finish off here by saying that the issue of Ibn Taymiyyah and his position has caused much controversy, as Ibn Taymiyyah typically always does. SubhanAllah, mashallah, Ibn Taymiyyah is the person I admire the most in all of Islamic history, and it is also true to say he generated so much controversy while he was alive and even until our times. Not all controversy is bad, by the way. Hint, hint.

And of course Ibn Taymiyyah is very interesting. SubhanAllah, I just have to say this here: his followers, and I have gently criticized many of his followers, some of his followers today, they did not like the fact that Ibn Taymiyyah might have denied the eternality of Jahannam, because this is something that you don't find in any person before Ibn Taymiyyah. So some of the modern people of that movement who claim to follow Ibn Taymiyyah denied that Ibn Taymiyyah ever said this. And they say this book is a fabrication, and they say he could never have said this, and there are massive debates within that movement whether he said it or not.

And I find this so interesting, that they have constructed an image of Ibn Taymiyyah that even Ibn Taymiyyah could not live up to. If you understand what I'm talking about; if not, then don't worry about it. But the image that they have of their version of Islam is so unreal that even their own scholar that they look up to could not live up to their own interpretation of that image.

And also, of course I admire Ibn Taymiyyah immensely, even though I'm not a blind follower and I respectfully disagree with some minor things. But one thing I love about Ibn Taymiyyah: he didn't care what anybody thought, and he spoke what he believed to be the truth, even if, and this is a key point, even if pretty much everybody before him said something else. And he seems to be one of the first people breaking away from a vast majority of scholarship, but he feels the Qur'an and Sunnah say something else. Simply because 99.9% of the people before him said something didn't mean anything to him. And to me, that requires intellectual bravery. Whether you agree or disagree, this is an independent mindset.

And I hope that also contextualizes a little bit of other things, without going too detailed. Whether that is true or not, Allah will be the judge in the akhirah, and history will be the judge in this world as well. But I agree with this point 100%: so what if 99.9% of the people before you said it? It doesn't make it the haqq, with a capital H.

And if you look at his position on the triple talaq, for example (we'll talk about that one day, because that was a question also), Ibn Taymiyyah was the first faqih, the first 'alim, to publicly state the triple talaq cannot be triple. And this is the fatwa that even Azhar now is adopting, and other institutions are adopting, because they realize the world is a very difficult place if you follow this position. We'll get to the issue of triple talaq. Ibn Taymiyyah was the one who said this, that now is becoming the standard position, even though none of the mainstream scholars before him said that.

So in any case, if you want further reading, there is actually a book published by Oxford, a collection of articles (you also have my article published in there), and the title of the book is "Islam and the Fate of Others," by Muhammad Hassan Khalil. And there is an entire chapter about Ibn Taymiyyah's view about Jahannam, and there's also a chapter about my view about salvation. You will find it in that book.
